```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(ggridges)
library(patchwork)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.width = 6,
  fig.asp = .6,
  out.width = "90%"
)

theme_set(theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom"))
```

## Problem 1

```{r}
data("ny_noaa")

ny_noaa_df = 
  ny_noaa |> 
  separate(date, into = c("year", "month", "day"), sep = "-") |> 
  mutate(
    across(c(year, month, day), as.integer),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10)
```

The `ny_noaa` dataset contains daily weather observations from
`r n_distinct(pull(ny_noaa_df, id))` weather stations in New York State
between 1981 and 2010, with `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations of
`r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables in the raw data. Each row is one station on one
day. The variables are a station `id`, the `date` of observation,
precipitation (`prcp`), snowfall (`snow`), snow depth (`snwd`), and maximum
and minimum temperature (`tmax` and `tmin`).

Missing data is a substantial issue. Temperature is missing for roughly 44% of
observations, snow depth for about 23%, snowfall for about 15%, and
precipitation for about 6%; this likely reflects that not all stations record
all measurements. In cleaning, I separated `date` into `year`, `month`, and
`day`, converted temperatures from tenths of a degree Celsius to degrees
Celsius, and converted precipitation from tenths of a millimeter to
millimeters. Snowfall and snow depth are already recorded in millimeters.

```{r}
ny_noaa_df |> 
  count(snow) |> 
  arrange(desc(n)) |> 
  head(10)
```

The most commonly observed snowfall value is 0, with over two million
observations. This makes sense because most days in New York State have no
snow at all; snowfall is only possible during winter months, so the majority
of days across the year record zero. The next most common values after 0 and
missing are 25, 13, 51, and 76 mm, which correspond to 1, 0.5, 2, and 3
inches. This suggests measurements were originally taken in inches and
converted, so values cluster at whole and half-inch increments.

```{r}
ny_noaa_df |> 
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |> 
  mutate(month = factor(month, levels = c(1, 7), labels = c("January", "July"))) |> 
  group_by(id, year, month) |> 
  summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |> 
  drop_na(mean_tmax) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = .3) + 
  geom_line(alpha = .3) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ month) + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1985, 1995, 2005)) + 
  labs(
    title = "Average max temperature in January and July by station",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean max temperature (C)")
```

January and July temperatures occupy entirely separate ranges, with January
station means mostly between -10 and 10°C and July means mostly between 20
and 30°C. Within each panel, stations move together from year to year: a cold
January is cold across nearly all stations at once, reflecting weather systems
that affect the whole state. There is substantial year-to-year variability but
no obvious warming trend across this 30-year window.

A few outliers stand out. In January, one station recorded a mean near -13°C
in the early 1980s and another near -12°C around 2004. In July, one station
recorded a mean near 14°C around 1988, well below every other July
observation, which likely reflects a recording error or an unusual station.

```{r, fig.width = 10}
tmax_tmin_plot = 
  ny_noaa_df |> 
  drop_na(tmax, tmin) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) + 
  geom_hex() + 
  labs(
    title = "Max vs min temperature",
    x = "Min temperature (C)",
    y = "Max temperature (C)")

snow_plot = 
  ny_noaa_df |> 
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = as.factor(year))) + 
  geom_density_ridges(scale = .85) + 
  scale_y_discrete(breaks = seq(1981, 2010, by = 5)) + 
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall distribution by year",
    x = "Snowfall (mm)",
    y = "Year")

tmax_tmin_plot + snow_plot
```

The hexbin plot shows a strong positive linear relationship between daily
minimum and maximum temperature, with most observations concentrated along a
band from roughly -10°C to 30°C. A scatterplot would be ineffective here
because 1.4 million points would overplot into a solid mass; binning shows
where the data actually concentrate. A handful of implausible observations sit
well off the main band, including points near 60°C and -40°C, which are likely
recording errors.

The snowfall distributions are stable across the thirty years, with no
apparent trend. Each year shows the same multimodal shape, with peaks at
roughly 25, 50, and 76 mm, again the 1-, 2-, and 3-inch values, reflecting
that measurements were recorded in inches and converted.

## Problem 2

```{r}
nhanes_demo = 
  read_csv("./data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  filter(age >= 21) |> 
  drop_na() |> 
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("male", "female")),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c("Less than high school", "High school equivalent", "More than high school")))

nhanes_accel = 
  read_csv("./data/nhanes_accel.csv") |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims") |> 
  mutate(minute = as.numeric(minute))

nhanes_df = 
  inner_join(nhanes_demo, nhanes_accel, by = "seqn")
```

The demographic file begins with four rows of codebook notes, so I skipped
those when importing. I excluded participants under 21 and those with missing
demographic data, which leaves `r n_distinct(pull(nhanes_df, seqn))`
participants. Sex and education were stored as numeric codes, so I converted
both to factors with informative labels, ordering education from least to
most. The accelerometer file stores one column per minute of the day, which is
not tidy; I pivoted these into a `minute` variable and a `mims` variable so
each row is one minute of observation for one participant. Joining the two
gives `r format(nrow(nhanes_df), big.mark = ",")` rows.

```{r}
nhanes_demo |> 
  count(education, sex) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = n) |> 
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r}
nhanes_demo |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age, fill = sex)) + 
  geom_density(alpha = .5) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ education) + 
  labs(
    title = "Age distribution by sex and education level",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Sex")
```

The More than high school category is the largest, with 115 participants, and
is roughly balanced between men and women. The Less than high school group is
also balanced, while the High school equivalent group has noticeably more men
than women (35 versus 23).

The age distributions differ by education level. Participants with less than a
high school education are concentrated at older ages, peaking near 70, and men
and women have similar distributions. In the high school equivalent group, men
skew younger than women, with a male peak near 30 and a female peak near 70.
Among participants with more than a high school education, both sexes are
younger overall, with a pronounced peak near age 30 that is stronger for
women.

```{r}
nhanes_df |> 
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, education) |> 
  summarize(total_activity = sum(mims), .groups = "drop") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = .5) + 
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ education) + 
  labs(
    title = "Total daily activity by age, sex, and education",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex")
```

Total daily activity declines with age across all three education levels,
though the shape of that decline differs. Among participants with less than a
high school education, activity falls fairly steadily from roughly 17,000 MIMS
in the twenties to about 9,000 by age 80, with men and women following similar
trajectories. In the high school equivalent group, activity peaks in the
thirties and forties, especially for women, who reach about 17,000 MIMS near
age 40, before dropping sharply after 60. Among those with more than a high
school education, activity stays relatively flat from the twenties through the
fifties before declining, and women are consistently more active than men
across most of the age range.

One participant in the More than high school group recorded total activity
near zero, which likely reflects a device malfunction or non-wear rather than
genuine inactivity.

```{r}
nhanes_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = minute, y = mims, color = sex)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = .05) + 
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ education) + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(360, 720, 1080), labels = c("6am", "12pm", "6pm")) + 
  labs(
    title = "24-hour activity profiles by education level and sex",
    x = "Time of day",
    y = "MIMS",
    color = "Sex")
```

All three education levels show the same basic circadian pattern: activity is
near zero overnight, rises steeply between about 5am and 8am, plateaus through
the day, and falls off after about 8pm. The overnight trough and daytime
plateau are consistent across groups, which is expected since sleep and waking
hours do not vary much by education.

The differences between groups are in the level and shape of the daytime
plateau. Participants with less than a high school education show a distinct
midday peak around noon, with women more active than men for most of the day.
In the high school equivalent group, the daytime profile is flatter and the
two sexes track each other closely. Among participants with more than a high
school education, the plateau is sustained later into the evening, and this
group shows the highest peak values overall, with some observations above 75
MIMS that do not appear in the other panels.
